Before we begin this evening's meeting, I'd like to acknowledge that February 1st marks the beginning of Black History Month,
a month dedicated to honouring the legacy, brilliance, and resilience of Black communities in Kitchener and across Canada.

This year's theme, celebrating 30 years of Black History Month, honouring Black brilliance across generations, from nation builders to tomorrow's visionaries, recognizes three decades of celebrating Black history in Canada.

In fact, yesterday we had the pleasure of seeing the Honourable Jean Augustine, the first Black woman elected as a Member of Parliament, in attendance at the launch of this month's events at the concealing Waterloo Region Museum.

This month reminds us of the countless ways Black Canadians have shaped this country through leadership, creativity, innovation, and an enduring strength that has carried communities through generations.
Their contributions continue to influence our city today and will guide and inspire the generations that follow.
Black History Month is also a time to reflect and be honest about the work that still needs to be done.
It calls on all of us to recommit to building a city where equity, belonging and human rights are not just ideals, but everyday practices.
That includes acknowledging and confronting anti-Black racism, both in historical roots and the ways it continues to show up in our systems, institutions and daily lives.
A true sense of belonging means that people feel seen, valued and safe, not only during moments of recognition, but in ordinary everyday spaces of life.
It means creating a community where Black residents can thrive, contribute, and be their whole authentic selves without barriers.
I encourage everyone to use this month as an opportunity to learn more about Black Canadian history and reflect on the challenges and accomplishments of Black Canadians.
I invite you to learn, participate, and celebrate.
Whether through local community events throughout the month, storytelling, food, music, or reflection, there are so many different ways to engage.
Let us all commit to building a Kitchener and a world where everyone feels they belong and where every person has the freedom to live with dignity, pride, and possibility.
And now please join me and our council as we listen to the Hymn of Freedom to honor and celebrate the perseverance, strength and rich heritage of African, Caribbean and Black members of our country.

and members of Council. I'm pleased to share that the City of Kitchener has been recognized with the
Provincial Age-Friendly Recognition Award. This honour reflects our ongoing commitment to creating
a city where people of all ages and abilities can thrive. This recognition celebrates communities
across Ontario that are leading in accessibility, inclusion, and age-friendly planning. It reminds
us that when we design a community that supports older adults, we create places that work for
everyone. This recognition would not have been possible without Council support
through the 2023 budget. Before this investment, the City-led older adult
programs were offered in just five community centres. With Council support
and the dedication of our staff team, we are now delivering program in 13
community centres as well as Grand River Recreation Complex and Dune Valley Golf
Course. The growth has been significant. Previously we offered between 90 and
115 programs per session and I'm pleased to report that this upcoming
spring we will be offering 384 programs but expansion was only part of this work
and ensuring people are aware of the available opportunities was another
challenge we set out to overcome. Through engagement with older adults in the
community we heard that finding information was difficult. In response
we worked collaboratively with older adults to co-create our older adult
Services Program Guide. This guide makes information easier to access, easier to
understand, and a format that meets their needs. Most importantly, it helps older
adults learn about programs and services available right in their own
neighborhoods. It is evident that this work is making a real difference. Older
adults tell us they feel more connected, more active, and more supported. They see
themselves reflected in their community and feel welcomed in our centers and
spaces. This is what an age-friendly city looks like in action. Tonight I would like to sincerely
thank Council for recognizing the importance of this work and for investing in a more accessible
and inclusive future. This provincial honor reflects Kitchener's commitment to supporting
residents at every age and every stage of life. Thank you for your continued leadership and
support as we build a community where we can all live well and age well.
